questions.body: In ACID, what does the "I" for isolation guarantee?

options.text: Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work
A transaction either fully happens or not at all

questions.explanation: Isolation makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another, to the degree of the chosen isolation level. Durability is about surviving crashes and atomicity about all-or-nothing.
questions.interview_line: Isolation levels are a dial between correctness and concurrency.

questions.body: Which mechanisms are used to provide atomicity and durability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Undo and redo of log records on recovery
Forcing the log to disk before commit returns

questions.explanation: The log is written first, flushed before a commit is acknowledged, and replayed or undone at recovery. Denormalisation is a schema design choice unrelated to either.
questions.interview_line: Write-ahead logging is why a commit can be fast and still durable.

questions.body: Which isolation level is the weakest one that still prevents dirty reads?
questions.explanation: Read committed only lets a transaction see committed data, which stops dirty reads. Non-repeatable reads and phantoms need the stronger levels.
questions.interview_line: Read committed is the default in many databases for a reason: it is cheap and avoids the worst anomaly.

questions.body: A table is in 2NF but has a non-key column that depends on another non-key column. Which normal form does it violate?
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency of a non-key column on the key through another non-key column violates third normal form. 2NF only removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key.
questions.interview_line: Every non-key attribute should depend on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.

questions.body: Denormalising a schema can make reads faster at the cost of duplicate data and harder updates.
questions.explanation: Copying data avoids joins, which speeds reads, but every copy must be kept consistent on writes. It is a deliberate trade-off, not a default.
questions.interview_line: Normalise first, then denormalise where measurements show the joins hurt.

questions.body: How does a primary key differ from a unique constraint in standard SQL?

options.text: A table can have only one primary key, and its columns cannot be NULL
A unique constraint can only cover one column

questions.explanation: A table has at most one primary key and its columns are never NULL. It may have many unique constraints, which can span several columns.
questions.interview_line: The primary key identifies a row; unique constraints enforce other business rules.

questions.body: Why do most database indexes use a B+ tree rather than a binary search tree?

options.text: A high fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so few disk pages are read per lookup
B+ trees are smaller than the table itself

questions.explanation: Each node is a disk page holding hundreds of keys, so a lookup touches only a handful of pages, and leaves are linked for fast range scans.
questions.interview_line: B+ trees are built around disk page reads, not around comparisons.

questions.body: Which statements about adding an index are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It can speed up reads that filter or sort on the indexed columns
It slows down inserts and updates on those columns
It always makes every query faster

questions.explanation: An index speeds the queries it fits, but every write must also maintain it and it takes space. It does nothing for queries that cannot use it.
questions.interview_line: Index for the queries you run, not for every column.

questions.body: In a LEFT JOIN from A to B, what do you get for a row of A that has no match in B?

options.text: The row appears with NULLs for B's columns

questions.explanation: A left join keeps every row of the left table; where the right side has no match its columns are NULL. An inner join would drop the row.
questions.interview_line: Use a left join when absence is meaningful, an inner join when it is not.

questions.body: A condition on an aggregate such as COUNT(*) > 3 goes in the ____ clause, not WHERE.
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot see aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
questions.interview_line: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups.

questions.body: Two transactions that each hold a lock the other needs form a deadlock, and a database resolves it by aborting one of them.
questions.explanation: The database detects the cycle in its wait-for graph (or times out) and rolls back a victim so the other can proceed. The application should retry the aborted transaction.
questions.interview_line: Keep transactions short and take locks in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks.

questions.body: What is the main benefit of multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)?

options.text: Readers do not block writers, and writers do not block readers
It removes the need for a transaction log
It makes all queries serializable for free
It stores every row only once

questions.explanation: Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot of older row versions, so reads take no locks that block writes. The cost is keeping old versions around until they can be cleaned up.
questions.interview_line: MVCC trades storage and cleanup work for much better read concurrency.
